title: Paz y Administración: the General, the Desert, and the State He Left Standing
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Tucumán and the Colegio del Uruguay

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán, the colonel's son
stops.campa: A son is born in San Miguel de Tucumán to Colonel José Segundo Roca, veteran of the wars of independence, and is named Julio Argentino. The province is sugar country, and the house he is born into keeps soldiering as a trade the way other houses keep a shop. Within twenty-five years the father and at least one of the brothers will be dead in Paraguay. The boy will command the army that closes the last open frontier of the republic, and the country he leaves behind will carry his face on its hundred-peso note for most of a century.
suggested_refs: The Roca family properties near San Miguel de Tucumán, disputed between El Bracho and La Fronterita

stops.name: Concepción del Uruguay, the Colegio del Uruguay
stops.date_confidence: traditional; institutional history gives c. 1856-1857, month and day not established
stops.campa: He is sent across to Entre Ríos, to the Colegio Nacional that Urquiza founded on the Uruguay river, the school that turns out the political and military class of the coming republic in a single set of dormitories. Boys here learn Latin, artillery and each other, and the friendships and enmities formed in these corridors will be fought out across the pampa for the next thirty years. Roca leaves before he is fifteen with a commission in the army of the Confederation, which is at war with the province of Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The Colegio Nacional de Concepción del Uruguay, seedbed of the Generación del Ochenta
sources: Colegio Nacional Justicia Uruguay institutional history

stops.name: Cañada de Cepeda, the baptism of fire
stops.campa: At sixteen he stands with the Confederation guns in the Cañada del arroyo Cepeda, on the Santa Fe side of the Arroyo del Medio, twenty-five kilometres north of Pergamino. Urquiza breaks Mitre's line here and marches on Buenos Aires, and the peace that follows lasts two years. Roca is a commissioned artillery officer, teniente segundo, not a boy carrying his father's kit. His whole career will be fought inside the argument this field opens: whether the interior provinces or the port city gets to name the nation.
suggested_refs: The Cañada de Cepeda battlefield, 23 October 1859, on the Santa Fe bank of the Arroyo del Medio

stops.name: Pavón, promoted on the losing field
stops.campa: Two years later the same two armies meet again near the estancia of Domingo Palacios, between Rueda and Godoy, forty kilometres south of Rosario. Urquiza's cavalry wins its wing and then rides off the field, leaving the infantry to Mitre; the Confederation loses the war it had won at Cepeda. Roca is there, on the beaten side, and is made teniente primero in the hours after the defeat. The republic will now be built outward from Buenos Aires, and the officer who finishes building it learns the lesson in the wrong uniform.
suggested_refs: The Pavón battlefield near the Domingo Palacios estancia, 17 September 1861

stops.name: Salta, the National Guard regiment
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, and the pool gives only the province
stops.campa: He is given command of a National Guard regiment in Salta, in the northwest, the province his family has served in and will bury men from. Paraguay declares war on Argentina this year and the northern regiments march. He is an officer of the line in a country that has just finished fighting itself and is about to spend five years fighting a neighbour. The Salta battalion he trains here will follow him into the swamps above the Paraná and come back at half its strength.
suggested_refs: The Salta National Guard regiment of 1865, nucleus of Roca's Paraguayan service

stops.name: Tuyutí, sargento mayor at twenty-two
stops.campa: North of Paso de Patria, on the flat ground the allies call Tuyutí, Solano López throws his army against the allied camp in the largest pitched battle ever fought in South America, and some nine thousand Paraguayans die in an afternoon. Roca is in the line with the Salta troops and is promoted sargento mayor at twenty-two for what he does there. The war teaches a generation of Argentine officers that rails, telegraph and massed infantry beat courage, and it is this generation, not their fathers, who will take Patagonia.
suggested_refs: The Tuyutí battlefield, 2 km north of Paso de Patria, 24 May 1866

stops.name: Curupayty, half the Salta battalion
stops.campa: Eight kilometres from Humaitá the allies walk into the trenches at Curupayty behind a naval bombardment that has not touched them. Nine thousand men attack, four thousand fall in a few hours, and the war stops dead for a year. Roca leads the Salta battalion into it and loses half his force. Somewhere in this campaign his father, Colonel José Segundo Roca, dies, and with him a brother; the English record counts two brothers dead and the Spanish record counts one, and the family does not settle it.
suggested_refs: The Curupayty earthworks on the Paraguay river, 8 km from Humaitá
sources: Wikipedia, 'Julio Argentino Roca' (English and Spanish, which disagree on the number of brothers)

stops.name: Pastos Grandes, Varela broken in the Puna
stops.date_confidence: attested; 12 January in most accounts, 14 January in some, and the coordinate is an approximation of the salar
stops.campa: The last of the federal caudillos, Felipe Varela, has been raiding the northwest with a montonera the national army cannot catch. Roca, now lieutenant colonel, brings reinforcements up from Jujuy and Salta into the Puna, four thousand metres above the sea, and Varela's people are broken at Pastos Grandes in the January glare and the thin air. The armed resistance of the interior to Buenos Aires effectively ends on this salt flat. The officers who close it will be handed the south as their next assignment.
suggested_refs: The Combate de Pastos Grandes, Puna de Salta, January 1869

stops.name: Ñaembé, the colonelcy at twenty-eight
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate near Goya is an approximation
stops.campa: Ricardo López Jordán has killed Urquiza and raised Entre Ríos, and the national army runs him down in Corrientes at the Ñaembé stream near Goya. Roca's part in it is decisive and he is made colonel the same day, at twenty-eight. Three provincial risings have now been put down by the same young officer in six years. The caudillo wars are finished, and what is left of the map that the national state does not administer is the country south and west of the frontier ditch. The war ministry knows it.
suggested_refs: The Ñaembé battlefield near Goya, Corrientes, 26 January 1871

stops.name: Córdoba, the marriage to Clara Funes
stops.campa: In Córdoba he marries Clara Funes, eighteen, daughter of the estanciero Tomás Funes and Eloísa Díaz. The marriage ties the Tucumán officer into the Córdoba landed families who will run the political machine of the next thirty years; his wife's sister Elisa marries Miguel Juárez Celman, who will follow him into the presidency. They have six children by the count of the Archivo General de la Nación and seven by the count of Wikipedia, among them Julio Argentino Pascual Roca, a future vice president of the republic.
suggested_refs: The Funes family of Córdoba, hinge of the Partido Autonomista Nacional
sources: Archivo General de la Nación (six children) against Wikipedia (seven)

stops.name: Río Cuarto, the southern frontier of Córdoba
stops.date_confidence: period attested c. 1873-1878; the start year is used and the month defaulted
stops.campa: He takes the frontier command on the southern edge of Córdoba province, at Río Cuarto, where the settled country stops and the Ranquel raiding country begins. The work is patrols, forts, stolen cattle, captives recovered and captives not recovered, a war of small columns that produces no battle anyone names. He spends five years learning the wells, the horses, the grass and the distances of a country the Buenos Aires ministries have printed on their maps and have never crossed.
suggested_refs: The Córdoba frontier line and its fortines, 1870s
sources: Roca military service record as cited in standard biographies

stops.name: Santa Rosa, Mendoza, coronel mayor at thirty-one
stops.campa: Nicolás Avellaneda has been president since October when Mitre's people rise against the election that put him there. Roca marches on Mendoza and breaks General José Miguel Arredondo at Santa Rosa, ending the revolt. Avellaneda promotes him on the field to coronel mayor, then the highest rank below general, at thirty-one. Two weeks earlier a small government force had held the estancia La Verde against Mitre himself. Roca is not there, though the two victories are told together.
suggested_refs: The Santa Rosa battlefield, Mendoza, 7 December 1874
The action at estancia La Verde, 26 November 1874, fought without Roca

stops.name: Villa Mercedes, the Fifth Division
stops.date_confidence: period attested 1875-1877; the start year is used and the month defaulted
stops.campa: From Villa Mercedes in San Luis he commands the Fifth Division and turns it into an instrument rather than a garrison: remounts, telegraph, forward depots, officers who know the water. Alsina, the war minister, is meanwhile digging a ditch across the pampa to keep the raiders out, and has pushed the line as far as Carhué. Roca's position is that a ditch defends nothing and that the frontier should be carried in one movement to the Río Negro. He is asking, in substance, for the ministry.
suggested_refs: The Zanja de Alsina and the frontier line at Carhué, 1876
Roca's official military correspondence from Villa Mercedes
sources: Roca's official military correspondence, cited in standard biographies

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Ministry of War and Navy
stops.campa: Avellaneda gives him the war ministry at thirty-four. Congress has an unexecuted law on its books from 1867, Ley 215, ordering the frontier carried to the Río Negro; in August Avellaneda sends up the bill to enforce it and in October Congress votes one million six hundred thousand pesos. Sarmiento had written the argument thirty-three years before in Facundo, civilization against barbarism, and this office is where the argument acquires a budget, a rail schedule and five columns of cavalry.
suggested_refs: Ley 215 of 23 August 1867 and Ley 947 of October 1878, the legislative spine of the campaign

stops.name: Trenque Lauquen, one of five columns
stops.campa: The campaign opens. Five columns leave the frontier line on the same day, one of them from the fort at Trenque Lauquen, and converge south and west on the Río Negro and the Neuquén. A year of preliminary raiding has already taken prisoners and recovered captives. Behind them stands a book: Estanislao Zeballos has written La conquista de quince mil leguas and given it to the war minister for nothing, and it will be taken for Roca's own for a century. The country ahead has never belonged to the republic except on paper.
suggested_refs: Estanislao Zeballos, La conquista de quince mil leguas (1878, corrected ed. 1879), dedicated to the War Minister
sources: Wikisource, 'La conquista de quince mil leguas / Oríjen de esta obra'

stops.name: Choele Choel, the twenty-fifth of May on the river
stops.campa: On the island of Choele Choel in the Río Negro the expedition keeps the national holiday: reveille, the flag raised, the military band, a mass said on the bank six hundred kilometres beyond the old frontier. The same day Roca telegraphs the interim war minister the tally of an action fought nearby, eighteen dead and twenty taken prisoner, four of them captive women, the arithmetic of a holiday kept at gunpoint on ground the army has not finished taking.
stops.quote: Se han abatido dos grupos de indios que se preparaban para dar malón, muertos 18 y tomados 20 como prisioneros, entre ellos cuatro cautivas.
stops.quote_source: Roca's telegram to the interim Minister of War, Choele Choel, 25 May 1879, recorded by Col. Manuel José Olascoaga, Estudio topográfico de la Pampa y Río Negro (1880), quoted in La Izquierda Diario
suggested_refs: Olascoaga, Estudio topográfico de la Pampa y Río Negro (1880), the campaign's own record
sources: La Izquierda Diario, 'A 141 años. El 25 de mayo de 1879'

stops.name: Choele Choel, the letter about the desert
stops.date_confidence: traditional; 2 June 1879 in the reachable accounts, no archival original located, and the wording varies between them
stops.campa: A week after the flag-raising, following a religious ceremony on the Río Negro, Roca writes to President Avellaneda a line that will be quoted for a century both in defence of the campaign and against it. The desert he means is not empty. It holds the Mapuche and Ranquel nations, their herds, their salt roads and their long treaties with a state that has decided to stop keeping them. Lautaro fought the same people's war three centuries earlier on the Chilean side of the cordillera, and it is closed here.
stops.quote: en ninguna parte se siente uno tan cerca de Dios como en el desierto
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a letter from Roca to President Avellaneda, Choele Choel, 2 June 1879; wording as given by Infobae, 16 April 2022. A variant runs: En ninguna parte como en el desierto se siente uno mas cerca de Dios.
suggested_refs: The disputed Choele Choel letter of 2 June 1879, known only through secondary quotation
sources: elarcondelahistoria.com, 'La campaña al desierto del General Roca (1879/1885)'

stops.name: Fisque Menuco, the fort that takes his name
stops.campa: The column reaches Fisque Menuco in the upper valley of the Río Negro and a fort goes up. It will be called Fuerte General Roca and then simply General Roca, a town of orchards and packing sheds in a valley of irrigated fruit, and the name will still be under argument a hundred and forty years later. The Tehuelche and Mapuche herds of this country are being driven off it. Three decades on a breeder buys the last good criollo mares from a cacique on the Chubut steppe, and Aimé Tschiffely rides two of them to New York.
suggested_refs: Fuerte General Roca, founded June 1879 on the upper Río Negro
sources: Municipal and provincial founding records of General Roca, Río Negro

stops.name: The confluence of the Limay and the Neuquén
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate for the junction is an approximation
stops.campa: Roca reaches the point where the Limay and the Neuquén meet and become the Río Negro, the geographical objective of the whole design, and a garrison is left to hold the crossing against passage from the south. In eight weeks the republic has taken possession of a territory larger than France at almost no cost in its own soldiers. The Argentine state now runs unbroken to the Andes and the Atlantic, and the question of what is owed to the people who were living on it is postponed for a century.
suggested_refs: The Limay and Neuquén confluence, reached 11 June 1879, southern anchor of the new frontier

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the election of April
stops.campa: He leaves the war ministry in October 1879 and runs for president as the candidate of the Partido Autonomista Nacional, the alliance of the interior provinces against the port. The electoral colleges give him the country decisively. Carlos Tejedor, governor of Buenos Aires, has been arming the provincial militia for months and does not accept the result. The soldier who has just annexed Patagonia is about to spend his last weeks as a general fighting inside the city he means to govern from.
suggested_refs: The Partido Autonomista Nacional and the presidential election of 11 April 1880

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Electoral College seats him
stops.campa: The Electoral College meets and elects him president, with Francisco Bernabé Madero as vice president. The national government has already withdrawn from the city to Belgrano, and province and nation each hold an armed force in the same streets. This is the axis Belgrano walked in 1806, when the English were thrown out of Buenos Aires by its own inhabitants, and the question now being settled with artillery is the one left open ever since: whether the city belongs to its province or to the country.
suggested_refs: The Electoral College session of 12-13 June 1880 and the government's removal to Belgrano

stops.name: Los Corrales and Puente Alsina, the answer in the streets
stops.campa: A week after the vote the fighting starts, and it starts because of the vote. National troops force the crossings at Los Corrales Viejos and Puente Alsina and take Barracas; the provincial forces hold for two days and ask for terms on the twenty-fourth. About three thousand men are dead in the suburbs of a city of three hundred thousand. It is the last armed revolt of a province against the nation in Argentine history. Tejedor resigns, and the presidency Roca won in April is now also a presidency he has taken.
suggested_refs: The battles of Los Corrales Viejos and Puente Alsina, 20-21 June 1880
sources: José María Rosa and standard accounts of the Revolución de 1880

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ley 1029 takes the capital
stops.campa: Congress sanctions Ley 1029 and the city of Buenos Aires becomes the federal capital, cut out of the province that founded it. Avellaneda is still president when this is done, three weeks before the handover, so the settlement Roca will govern under and be credited with is inherited rather than enacted by him. A week later he is promoted brigadier general for the Río Negro campaign. The province, dispossessed of its capital, will now have to build itself another one out of open grass.
suggested_refs: Ley 1029 de Federalización, sanctioned under Avellaneda, September 1880

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the inauguration
stops.campa: He takes the oath at thirty-seven, the youngest president the republic has had, and tells Congress that the watchword of his government will be Peace and Administration. The two things he says preoccupy him above all others are the army and the lines of communication. Behind him lie Cepeda, Pavón, Curupayty, Pastos Grandes, Ñaembé, Santa Rosa, the Río Negro and Puente Alsina. Ahead lie twenty-four years in which nothing large happens in the republic without his consent.
stops.quote: Al tomar a mi cargo la administracion general del pais, dos preocupaciones principalmente me dominan sobre todas las demas: el Ejercito y las vias de comunicacion.
stops.quote_source: Julio A. Roca, inaugural address to Congress, Buenos Aires, 12 October 1880, as quoted by the Academia Nacional de la Historia, 'Roca, el constructor'
suggested_refs: Roca's inaugural address to Congress, 12 October 1880
sources: Academia Nacional de la Historia, 'Roca, el constructor'

stops.name: La Plata, the province builds itself a capital
stops.campa: On open pampa fifty kilometres from the capital it has lost, the province of Buenos Aires founds a new one. Dardo Rocha, the governor, lays the stone; Pedro Benoit draws the plan, a perfect square crossed by diagonals with a park every six blocks. It is a provincial act and not a national one, though Roca's name gets attached to it. The city goes up in four years, the most complete surviving piece of physical evidence for what the Generación del Ochenta believed a state was: a grid laid over grass.
suggested_refs: The founding decree of La Plata, 19 November 1882, and Pedro Benoit's plan
sources: Founding decree and official history of La Plata

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ley 1532 and the National Territories
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the verified pool; standard accounts date the law 16 October 1884
stops.campa: Ley 1532 organizes what the columns took into nine National Territories: Misiones, Formosa, Chaco, La Pampa, Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego. Governors are appointed from Buenos Aires and the inhabitants elect nobody. Rails and telegraph go out to them on borrowed money, and the last of the nine does not become a province until 1990. Sixty-three years after this law a president nationalizes the British companies that laid the track, and Juan Perón calls it completing the country.
stops.quote: Con estos agentes poderosos de la civilizacion se ha afianzado la unidad nacional, se ha vencido y exterminado el espiritu de la montonera...
stops.quote_source: Julio A. Roca on the railways, inaugural address to Congress, Buenos Aires, 12 October 1880, as quoted by the Academia Nacional de la Historia, 'Roca, el constructor'
suggested_refs: Ley 1532 de Territorios Nacionales, 1884
sources: Academia Nacional de la Historia, 'Roca, el constructor'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the gold window closes
stops.campa: Convertibility of the paper peso into gold at par, established in 1883, is suspended in January 1885. The executive orders the Banco Nacional to stop paying out against notes, and the reserves stop draining. The single currency of Ley 1130, the boundary settlement with Chile of 1881, the schools, the ports and the borrowed money are all one machine, and this is the first time it stalls. It stalls far harder in 1890, and the man in the chair then will be his wife's sister's husband.
suggested_refs: The suspension of convertibility, January 1885, and the Caja de Conversión

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the shot that misses
stops.campa: An attempt is made on his life in the capital and fails. He is in the last months of a first term that federalized nothing it did not inherit and settled nearly everything else: the currency, the nine territories, the Avellaneda law giving the universities their autonomy, and the frontier declared closed the year before with the objectives of the campaign officially met. Fighting in the south continues after the declaration. The state's paperwork and the state's violence keep different calendars.
suggested_refs: The Avellaneda Law of 25 June 1885 on university autonomy
The official closing of the Conquest of the Desert, 1885

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the handover to Juárez Celman
stops.date_confidence: attested; the raw pool gave 11 October, and Juárez Celman took office on the 12th
stops.campa: He hands the sash to Miguel Juárez Celman, his wife's sister's husband, chosen by him and elected by the machine. The Argentine word for what follows is the unicato, the rule of one man, and nobody agrees whether the one man is the president or the general standing behind him. Roca is forty-three and out of office for the first time in a decade. In four years the Revolución del Parque will bring the whole arrangement down, and he will be the man who negotiates the terms of its fall.
suggested_refs: The presidential succession of 12 October 1886 and the beginning of the unicato

segments.name: The Unicato and the Second Presidency

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Minister of the Interior under Pellegrini
stops.campa: The Revolución del Parque has failed in the streets and won in the Congress. Juárez Celman resigns and Carlos Pellegrini takes the presidency, and Roca comes back as Minister of the Interior, the office that runs the provinces, the police and the elections. He holds it nine months and leaves the machine repaired. For the rest of the decade he is neither president nor out of power, and in the summer of 1895 he covers the office himself for three months while José Evaristo Uriburu is ill.
suggested_refs: The Revolución del Parque of July 1890 and the Pellegrini cabinet

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the second inauguration
stops.campa: He is sworn in a second time, eighteen years after the first, into a country of five million people with a wheat export and an unsettled boundary with Chile that both general staffs are costing out. Ten months later a boy is born on calle Tucumán in this city, into a family with frontier officers in it, and Jorge Luis Borges will spend a writing life on the mythology of exactly that officer class. The boundary will go to arbitration in four years, and in the same year he will take the power to deport foreigners without trial.
suggested_refs: Roca's second inauguration, 12 October 1898

stops.name: Punta Arenas, the Abrazo del Estrecho
stops.campa: Roca sails to the Strait of Magellan and meets Federico Errázuriz of Chile aboard warships off Punta Arenas. The two presidents embrace on deck, the press of both countries prints the photograph, and the war the two armies have been budgeting for does not happen. Eighty-two years earlier San Martín took an Argentine army over the Andes to make Chile independent; the boundary between the two republics he separated is what these two men are arguing about, at the far southern end of both of them.
suggested_refs: The Abrazo del Estrecho, 15 February 1899, off Punta Arenas
sources: Diplomatic record of the 1899 Argentine-Chilean meeting

stops.name: Ascochinga, the summers at La Paz
stops.date_confidence: the Thays park is dated 1901; the summers span the last two decades of the century, and the coordinate near Ascochinga is an approximation
stops.campa: Sixty kilometres north of Córdoba, in the Sierras Chicas, the estancia La Paz is where he spends his summers, and in 1901 Charles Thays lays out its park. His autumns are at La Larga on the Daireaux plain in Buenos Aires province. The two properties are the ordinary furniture of the class the campaign created: land opened in the south and the centre, distributed in large lots to the men who took it and the men who financed it, and then worked up into a French idea of a garden.
suggested_refs: Estancia La Paz, Ascochinga, and the park designed by Charles Thays in 1901
sources: La Nación, 'Los veranos cordobeses de Julio Argentino Roca'

stops.name: Buenos Aires and Santiago, the Pactos de Mayo
stops.campa: The May Pacts are signed: general arbitration by the British crown, naval limitation, and an end to the arms race that has been eating both budgets. Chile keeps its coast, Argentina keeps its Atlantic, and the boundary treaty of 1881 finally holds. The same government has just introduced compulsory military service, so the peace arrives with conscription attached to it. The bronze of the cannon neither country now needs is cast into a Christ and set on the watershed between them.
suggested_refs: The Pactos de Mayo, 28 May 1902, and the Cristo Redentor de los Andes
sources: Pactos de Mayo, 1902, official diplomatic archives

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ley 4144 and the Residence Law
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the verified pool; standard accounts date the law 22 November 1902
stops.campa: The Residence Law gives the executive power to expel any foreigner it judges dangerous to public order, without trial, and it is used at once against the anarchist and socialist organizers of the port and the printing shops. Argentina has spent twenty years importing the men who load its wheat and now legislates against their unions. The law stays on the books until 1958. In 1880 Roca had told Congress plainly what he intended to do with the powers the Constitution put in his hands.
stops.quote: emplearé todos los resortes y facultades que la Constitución ha puesto en manos del Poder Ejecutivo para evitar, sofocar y reprimir cualquier tentativa contra la paz pública.
stops.quote_source: Julio A. Roca, inaugural address to Congress, Buenos Aires, 12 October 1880, as quoted on gentedelpasado.blogspot.com
suggested_refs: Ley 4144 de Residencia, 1902, in force until 1958

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Drago Doctrine
stops.date_confidence: month attested (December 1902); standard accounts date the note 29 December 1902
stops.campa: Britain, Germany and Italy blockade Venezuela to collect on defaulted bonds. Roca's foreign minister, Luis María Drago, sends Washington a note arguing that public debt can never justify armed intervention by one state in the territory of another, and the argument enters international law under his name. The government that has just given itself the power to deport foreigners without trial is the same government telling the great powers they may not shell a debtor's ports.
suggested_refs: The Drago note of December 1902 to the United States government

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the pension law and the last message
stops.campa: A national retirement-fund law is enacted, the foundation the Argentine social security system will be built on. In May he had opened the congressional sessions with an inventory of the country he is about to hand over. On the twelfth of October Manuel Quintana takes the oath and Roca walks out of the Casa Rosada as president for the last time, sixty-one years old, having governed the republic for twelve years and arranged its government for most of another twelve.
stops.quote: No hay una sola región del país, por apartada que esté, en la cual no se haya inaugurado, o no esté en vías de construcción, una escuela primaria o superior, o de enseñanza agrícola, un ferrocarril, un camino, un puente, un puerto, una línea telegráfica, un hospital, un cuartel...
stops.quote_source: Julio A. Roca, address opening the congressional sessions, Buenos Aires, 1 May 1904, quoted (citing Miguel Ángel De Marco) by the Academia Nacional de la Historia, 'Roca, el constructor'
suggested_refs: The retirement-fund law of 20 September 1904
Roca's message opening the sessions of 1 May 1904
sources: Academia Nacional de la Historia, 'Roca, el constructor'

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, special ambassador
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established
stops.campa: Roque Sáenz Peña, who has just given Argentina the secret and compulsory ballot that will finish the machine Roca built, sends the old general to Rio de Janeiro as special ambassador. The mission is the Brazilian relationship, the other half of the South Atlantic. He is sixty-nine and has outlived his own political system; the Radicals will win the first clean election four years after he dies. He comes back to Buenos Aires in 1914, to a country that no longer needs him to arrange anything.
suggested_refs: Roca's special embassy to Brazil, 1912, under the Sáenz Peña presidency

stops.name: Estancia La Larga, Daireaux, the consul's novel
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the 1917 dedication; the visit is placed before October 1914
stops.campa: He invites a Druze emir out to La Larga to finish a book. Emín Arslán, once Ottoman consul in Buenos Aires and now an Argentine man of letters, spends part of a season on the Daireaux plain writing Final de un idilio, a novel of Belgium invaded, and says so himself in the dedication. Roca is seventy, the country's great pacifier of the pampas by the consul's phrase, sitting on land the pacification opened. He dies in October 1914; the novel appears in 1917, dedicated to his memory.
suggested_refs: Emín Arslán, Final de un idilio (1917), dedicated to the memory of Julio A. Roca

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death at seventy-one
stops.date_confidence: attested; the exact address of the residence varies between sources
stops.campa: Julio Argentino Roca dies in Buenos Aires at seventy-one, ten weeks into the European war that will make Argentine wheat indispensable and Argentine politics unrecognizable. He has been a cadet of the Confederation, an officer in Paraguay, the man who took Patagonia, twice president, and for thirty years the arbiter of who else could be. The republic buries him as a head of state. Nobody inherits the position he actually held, which was never an office and had no name in the constitution.
suggested_refs: The Roca residence in Buenos Aires, where he died on 19 October 1914

stops.name: Recoleta, the vault with his father
stops.date_confidence: month attested (October 1914); the exact burial day is not established
stops.campa: He is laid in the family vault in the Recoleta cemetery, a Mannerist front with wrought-iron gates worked in arabesques, angels and inverted torches, and a bronze bust of him that guides call the most severe face in the whole ground. His father, Colonel Segundo Roca of the independence wars, lies in the same vault. A few rows of tombs away, from 1976, lies Eva Perón, whose face will one day begin replacing his on the hundred-peso note. No relic legend attaches here. Nobody has ever come for the body.
suggested_refs: The Roca family vault, Cementerio de la Recoleta, Buenos Aires
sources: Foro de Baires, 'La tumba de Julio Argentino Roca'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the equestrian monument
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the inauguration day is not established
stops.campa: Three bronze figures on a base of polished red granite go up at the corner of Diagonal Sur and Perú, two blocks from the Casa Rosada, twenty-seven years after his death. The monument belongs to a deliberate campaign of the nineteen thirties and forties to build Roca into state patrimony; it is not the grief of 1914 arriving late. A decade that wanted a founder chose the one who had made the map. This bronze will become the most attacked public sculpture in the country.
suggested_refs: Monumento a Julio Argentino Roca, Buenos Aires, inaugurated 1941
SciELO Argentina, 'Julio A. Roca y la Conquista del desierto: monumentalización, patrimonio y usos del pasado'
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Monumento a Julio Argentino Roca (Buenos Aires)'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Roca genocida
stops.date_confidence: recurring and documented from the early 2000s onward; this date is a marker, not an event
stops.campa: The monument is painted, stoned, and written on again and again with two words: Roca genocida. Osvaldo Bayer runs a campaign called Desmonumentar, which asks that the statues come down, the streets be renamed, and a monument to indigenous women stand where this one stands. In 2012 a hundred-peso note with Eva Perón's face begins the phase-out of the note with Roca's. Nobody is arguing about what happened in 1879. The argument is about the man on the horse.
suggested_refs: Osvaldo Bayer's Desmonumentar campaign
The Evita 100-peso note, in circulation from 20 September 2012
sources: La Nación, 'Roca: el monumento más atacado'
Kalewche, 'Julio Argentino Roca: entre el bronce, el genocidio...'

stops.name: San Carlos de Bariloche, the monument that stays
stops.date_confidence: attested; the removal order and the judicial suspension are dated July and August 2023
stops.campa: The municipality orders the Roca monument moved off the centre of the Centro Cívico to the slopes above Lake Nahuel Huapi, citing the plaza renovation and decades of paint. A petition insists the monument is not to be touched, opposition politicians call the move an erasure of history, and the courts suspend the transfer. The statue does not move. He is still standing in a plaza in Mapuche country, in the province of the river he reached in June 1879, four hundred kilometres from the town that bears his name.
suggested_refs: The 2023 Centro Cívico refunctionalization project and the injunction that halted the transfer
